archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A quarterback whose best plays come when the pocket breaks down and he takes off, not from designed runs or from precision passing out of structure.

report.headline: Scrambles keep him afloat, but accuracy and sacks are sinking Miami's offense.
report.take:
Willis is Miami's starter for all four games, and the shape of his season is lopsided. When he leaves the pocket, he helps: 13 scrambles for 94 yards and 5 first downs at +0.53 EPA each, and his 112 rushing yards rank 6th among 42 qualifiers. When he stays in it and throws, he doesn't. His -0.153 passing EPA per dropback ranks 34th, his -9.2 CPOE ranks 38th, and his 16.5% bad-throw rate is 29th of 32. Miami is 0-4 and has scored 13, 13, 10 and 10 points.

The passing problem is mostly accuracy, not protection or play-calling. The clearest case is Week 3 against Kansas City. He was pressured on only 9.3% of dropbacks and took no sacks, yet still threw for -4 EPA on 36 attempts with a -7.1 CPOE. The deep ball is the worst of it: 5 completions on 24 throws of 20+ air yards, a CPOE of -19.2. The quick game behind the line is just as bad, at -0.4 EPA on 24 throws, even though three-quarters of them are caught. The one area that works is 10-19 yards, at +0.56 EPA on 19 throws. That is a small sample, but it is consistent with a passer who sees the field over the middle and misses on the touch throws at either end. He has also been far worse from shotgun (-0.258 EPA) than under center (+0.024), which suggests the play-action, run-first structure fits him better than spread dropbacks.

The sacks are who he is. A 9.6% sack rate and a 3.02-second time to throw look ugly, but his career pressure-to-sack rates were 43.5%, 66.7% and 60%. Those last two ranked at or near the bottom of the league. The 31% this year is actually tamer by his standards. It is the price of the scrambling, and the scrambles mostly pay for it. What they don't pay for is the situational damage: 6 sacks on 34 third-down plays, 3 sacks on 9 red-zone plays, and 3 fumbles with 2 lost. The Green Bay seasons are the counterpoint people will raise: 10.19 and 12.06 yards per attempt, CPOE of +6.9 and +22. Those came in five games of spot duty. The 2022 Titans line (4.53 YPA, -10.6 CPOE) looks much more like this one.

Where it goes from here depends on a supporting cast that just got thinner. De'Von Achane is on IR with a torn ACL, and that hurts the run game more than the passing game; his 12 targets produced essentially zero EPA. The receiver who matters is Caleb Douglas. His +0.35 EPA per target is the best on the team. He is listed out with an ankle, though the coach calls him day-to-day. Without him, Willis is leaning on Malik Washington, whose 28 targets have produced negative EPA. Expect a run-heavy plan built around Willis's legs, with modest passing totals and continued sack risk.

strengths.title: Scrambling turns broken plays positive
strengths.body: His 13 scrambles average +0.53 EPA and moved the chains five times, a better rate than almost anything he does as a passer. This is a stable trait: he ran for 123, 138 and 123 yards in tiny career samples. It is also why the sacks are tolerable. Designed runs (-0.33 EPA on 6) are not the same skill; the value comes from improvising.

strengths.title: Intermediate throws are working
strengths.body: On throws of 10-19 air yards he is at +0.56 EPA with a 57.9% success rate and near-neutral accuracy (-0.8 CPOE). That is the one depth where his ball placement matches the throw. On 19 attempts it is a hint rather than a fact, but it points to where Miami should build the passing game.

strengths.title: Better under center than in gun
strengths.body: From under center he is roughly average (+0.024 EPA, 41.4% success); from shotgun he is at -0.258. In an offense that passes 9.4 points less than expected, the play-action, under-center looks suit him. This is a scheme lever more than a flaw.

concerns.title: Accuracy is the core problem
concerns.body: A -9.2 CPOE (38th) and 16.5% bad-throw rate come from misses, not pressure. Week 3 against KC, with almost no pressure, was still negative. The deep ball (20.8% completions, -19.2 CPOE) is the worst of it. The 2022 Titans CPOE of -10.6 suggests this is his baseline, not a slump.

concerns.title: Sacks and fumbles in key spots
concerns.body: Holding the ball is a career-long trait; his pressure-to-sack rates of 66.7% and 60% ranked at the bottom in Green Bay. The sacks themselves are a cost of the scrambling. The real damage is where they land: 6 on third down, 3 on 9 red-zone plays, and 2 lost fumbles. That timing is why drives stall at 10-13 points.

concerns.title: Thin targets after Achane, Douglas
concerns.body: Achane is out for the season and Douglas, his most efficient target, is listed out. That leaves Washington, at -0.049 EPA on a team-high 28 targets, as the focal point. The screen and checkdown game was already failing at -0.4 EPA behind the line.

trend.note: His fantasy output has dropped every week (16.7, 12.5, 10, 2.5), bottoming out at -12.4 passing EPA on 17 attempts against the league's top defense in his first game without Achane. Week 2, his only positive passing game, came on a short, low-aggression plan (6.4 intended air yards).

nextGame.headline: Bengals' pass rush meets a QB who already takes sacks
nextGame.body:
Cincinnati's defense is 10th in EPA and 8th against the pass, and its 8.7% sack rate is 2nd in the league. That is the worst possible pairing for a quarterback whose sack rate already ranks 37th. There are openings, though. The Bengals rank 30th in EPA allowed on short throws and 25th in explosive run rate allowed, and they surrender 289 passing yards a game to quarterbacks (27th). But they give up only 1.25 touchdowns a game to the position (5th fewest), so yardage may come without points. The script is the other problem: Cincinnati leads the league in pass rate over expected, and Miami's pass defense ranks 29th. If the Bengals build a lead, Willis gets pushed into catch-up passing, where he has been at -0.15 EPA with both his interceptions.

Availability cuts both ways. Cincinnati's secondary is depleted: safety Bryan Cook (78% of snaps) is out, nickel corner Jalen Davis is on IR, and Kyle Dugger is out. That should open the intermediate middle, his best area. Defensive tackle B.J. Hill being out removes some interior push. On offense, Ja'Marr Chase (concussion) and Tee Higgins (groin) are both questionable; if either sits, the Bengals' ability to run away with the game shrinks. For Miami, Douglas's status is the swing. The coach calls him day-to-day despite the Out listing, and without him and Achane the passing targets are thin.

keyMatchups.title: Sack-prone QB vs elite sack rate
keyMatchups.body: Willis has been hit or sacked on 16.7% of dropbacks, and Cincinnati gets home on 8.7% of opponent dropbacks, 2nd in the league. His long time to throw is a career trait, so expect this to show up in the box score. The danger is on third down and in the red zone, where his sacks have killed drives.

keyMatchups.title: Scrambles against leaky run fits
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati ranks 25th in explosive run rate allowed and 17th in rush EPA. Willis's scrambles (+0.53 EPA each) are his most reliable source of value. Broken pockets against this pass rush should create more of them.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted secondary, short-area softness
keyMatchups.body: With two safeties and a nickel corner unavailable, and the defense already 30th against short throws, Miami can scheme easy completions and 10-19 yard throws. Those are the depths where Willis is most functional. Whether he can hit them consistently is the open question, given his 16.5% bad-throw rate.

nextGame.watch: Whether Miami leans on under-center play-action and quick intermediate throws to blunt Cincinnati's pass rush, and whether Douglas plays to give him a target who produces.

restOfSeason.body:
The rushing floor is real. Scrambling has followed him through every career stop, and in a run-first offense now without Achane, his legs carry even more of the load. The passing is unlikely to improve much. The accuracy numbers match his 2022 Titans tape rather than the Green Bay cameos, and those cameos covered only five games combined. Some regression toward average is likely in his 1% touchdown rate and his red-zone collapse (9 plays), so a few more touchdowns should come. Sacks and fumbles, however, are a lasting cost of how he plays.

Expect 150-200 passing yards a game, with spikes tied to Douglas's health and opponents with weak secondaries. Rushing should run in the mid-20s to high-30s, and he should keep taking close to three sacks a game. If the offense stays bottom-three in success rate and the losses pile up, his hold on the job is the biggest variable. The dossier gives no backup information, so that is a risk rather than a forecast.
swingFactors: Whether Miami builds around under-center play-action
Sack and fumble damage in the red zone

bets.reason: He has a 9.6% sack rate (37th) and a career-long tendency to hold the ball. He now faces the league's 2nd-best sack rate, likely in a trailing script that forces more dropbacks.

Scrambles are his most efficient play. Cincinnati allows the 25th-worst explosive run rate, and its pass rush should flush him more often. The risk is a small-sample week like his 6- and 11-yard games.
He has 1 passing TD in four games and a -0.709 red-zone EPA. Cincinnati allows only 1.25 touchdowns a game to quarterbacks (5th fewest) even while giving up yardage.
Miami has scored 10-13 in every game, and three of its four games stayed under. The Chase and Higgins injuries could cap Cincinnati's side, though Miami's 29th-ranked pass defense is the risk.

confidence.note: Four games and 127 dropbacks, a career built on tiny samples, and Douglas and Chase availability unresolved.
